task_spec:
> Using the Global Weather Repository CSV, produce:
> 1. Two ranked bar charts of the **top 10 hottest cities**, one by average and one by single hottest measurement temperature (celsius)
> 2. Two ranked bar charts of the **top 10 hottest countries**, one by average and one by single hottest measurement temperature (celsius)
> 3. **Print the top 10 lists to the console** before plotting: for each of the 4 charts, print the ranked names and their temperature values (e.g., "1. Paris: 25.2 deg C")
> 4. A **100-word summary** for a non-technical audience explaining the rankings and any notable patterns
>
> Column reference: cities are in `location_name`, countries in `country`, temperature in `temperature_celsius`.

report_draft: The world's hottest cities and countries cluster in the Middle East and North Africa, but rankings shift dramatically by measurement type. By average temperature, Ar Riyadh leads at 45°C; by single hottest reading, Suva, Fiji Islands, records an exceptional 79.3°C—roughly 30°C above the next tier. This divergence is stark: only three cities (Abu Dhabi, Doha, Muscat) appear in both top-10 rankings. At the country level, five nations overlap, showing stronger agreement but still substantial divergence. A few country names appeared under different spellings in the data, which may affect exact rankings. The pattern is clear: Middle Eastern cities maintain consistently high averages, while tropical regions occasionally spike to extremes. Most persistently hot locations cluster in one region; the highest peaks scatter globally.

report_history.content: The world's hottest cities and countries cluster heavily in the Middle East and North Africa, but rankings shift dramatically depending on measurement type. By average temperature, Ar Riyadh leads globally at 45°C, with Middle Eastern and North African cities dominating the top ten. However, single hottest readings tell a different story: Suva, Fiji Islands, recorded an exceptional 79.3°C, far exceeding any other peak. The next tier—Kuwait City, Baghdad, and Djibouti—peaks around 46–49°C, showing the average and maximum lists diverge substantially. Only three cities (Abu Dhabi, Doha, Muscat) appear in both rankings, indicating persistently hot climates. At the country level, Saudi Arabia and surrounding nations hold average rankings, while Fiji Islands' extreme outlier dominates single-reading rankings. This pattern suggests that while Middle East locations maintain consistently high temperatures, tropical locations occasionally experience exceptional heat spikes.
